title: Death at Blackwood Manor
setting: A stormy evening at a remote English countryside manor, 1932

victim.name: Lord Reginald Blackwood
victim.description: The 62-year-old patriarch of the Blackwood family, found dead in his study at 10:15 PM. A half-finished glass of brandy sits on his desk. The doctor confirms poison — but the blow to the back of his head tells another story.

intro_narrative:
The rain hammers against the windows of Blackwood Manor as your motorcar pulls up the gravel drive. You are here at the request of the local constabulary — Lord Reginald Blackwood, one of the wealthiest men in the county, has been found dead in his locked study.

The doctor says poison. The bruise on the back of his skull says otherwise. The brandy glass on his desk is half-empty, and the fire in the hearth has burned down to embers.

Six people were in the manor tonight. One of them is a killer. The storm has cut the telephone lines and washed out the road — nobody is leaving until morning.

You have until dawn to solve this.

initial.prompt: Lady Eleanor sits by the drawing room fireplace, her eyes red but her composure intact. She clutches a handkerchief embroidered with violets.

choices.text: Where were you when your husband was found?
choices.response: I was in the drawing room all evening, reading. I heard nothing until Hartley — our butler — came running in, white as a sheet. He said Reginald wouldn't answer the study door. We broke it open together... and there he was.

clue.text: Lady Eleanor claims she was in the drawing room all evening reading. Says she heard nothing.

choices.text: Was your marriage a happy one?
choices.response: We had been married thirty-one years, Detective. Happiness comes and goes like the seasons. Reginald was... preoccupied these last months. Business troubles, I assumed. He wouldn't speak of it.

clue.text: Lady Eleanor hints at distance in the marriage. Lord B was 'preoccupied' recently.

choices.text: Your husband sent an urgent letter to his solicitor. He was changing his will — did you know?
choices.response: New will? What new will? Reginald's solicitor was here last Tuesday, yes, but my husband told me it was merely routine paperwork. Are you telling me he changed his will?

clue.text: Lady Eleanor appears genuinely surprised about a new will. Solicitor visited last Tuesday.

choices.text: The brandy glass — did your husband drink often?
choices.response: Every evening after dinner, without fail. Always the same — two fingers of brandy from the decanter in his study. Nobody else touched that decanter. It was his private ritual.

clue.text: Lord B drank brandy from his private study decanter every evening. Nobody else used it.

initial.prompt: Victor Blackwood, 34, stands by the window nursing a whisky. He's dressed expensively but his cufflinks don't match — one gold, one silver. His hands tremble slightly.

choices.text: Where were you this evening?
choices.response: I was in the billiards room until about half nine, then I went to the library to make a telephone call. Except the storm had already taken the lines down by then. I returned to the billiards room and that's where I was when the commotion started.

clue.text: Victor says he was in the billiards room, then went to the library to phone someone around 9:30. Lines were down.

choices.text: You said you tried to make a telephone call. Who were you trying to reach?
choices.response: My... my broker in London. I had some urgent financial matters to discuss. The markets have been rather unkind lately, if you must know.

clue.text: Victor has urgent financial problems. Needed to call his broker.

choices.text: You stand to inherit everything now.
choices.response: That's a ghastly thing to say while my father's body is still warm. Yes, I'm the eldest son. But Father was in excellent health — I expected him to outlive us all. Besides, I have my own income from the family trust.

clue.text: Victor is defensive about inheriting. Claims he has his own trust income.

choices.text: Those mismatched cufflinks — rough evening?
choices.response: I... I dressed in a hurry after dinner. I'd gone to my room to change and I was running late. It's nothing.

clue.text: Victor changed clothes hastily after dinner. Mismatched cufflinks suggest he was in a rush.

ask_victor_will.prompt: You mention the new will to Victor. His face goes pale.

choices.text: Your father changed his will last week. Did you know?
choices.response: Changed it? Changed it how? You mean... I thought the solicitor visit was about the estate taxes. If Father cut me out— no, no, he wouldn't. Would he? We had argued, yes, but that was weeks ago. About the money I borrowed from the company accounts. He was furious, but he said he'd forgiven me.

clue.text: Victor borrowed money from Lord B's company accounts. They argued about it. Victor fears being cut from the will.

initial.prompt: Margaret Blackwood, 28, sits on the stairs hugging her knees. She's been crying. There's a smudge of something dark — ink? — on her left hand.

choices.text: Where were you this evening, Margaret?
choices.response: I was writing letters in my room most of the evening. I came down around nine to get some stationery from the library, then went back upstairs. I didn't come down again until I heard the screaming.

clue.text: Margaret was writing letters upstairs. Went to the library for stationery around 9 PM.

choices.text: What's that on your hand?
choices.response: Ink. I was writing letters, as I said. I spilled the inkwell when I heard the noise downstairs. I'm afraid I'm rather clumsy when startled.

clue.text: Margaret has ink on her hand from writing letters. Claims she spilled it when startled.

choices.text: Were you close with your father?
choices.response: I adored him. He was the only one who supported my wish to study medicine. Mother thought it unladylike, Victor thought it a waste. Father even set aside money for my tuition at Edinburgh. I was to start in the autumn.

clue.text: Lord B was funding Margaret's medical studies. She was the only one he supported in her goals.

choices.text: Did you see anyone near the study this evening?
choices.response: When I went to the library for stationery... I thought I heard voices from the study. Two people, one of them Father. But the other voice — I couldn't tell. It might have been Dr. Crawford. He does have that low murmur.

clue.text: Margaret heard two voices in the study around 9 PM. One was Lord B, the other she couldn't identify but suggests Dr. Crawford.

ask_margaret_library.prompt: You ask Margaret about seeing Victor in the library.

choices.text: Victor says he went to the library around 9:30. You were there at 9. Did you see him?
choices.response: I left the library at about a quarter past nine. I didn't see Victor there. But when I was in the corridor upstairs, I did see him coming out of Father's study — not the library. It was about twenty past nine. He looked... agitated.

clue.text: Margaret saw Victor leaving Lord B's study around 9:20 PM, looking agitated. He claimed he was going to the library.

ask_margaret_argument.prompt: You ask Margaret about arguments in the family.

choices.text: Were there any big arguments recently between your father and Victor?
choices.response: About three weeks ago they had a terrible row. Father found out Victor had been taking money from the estate accounts — quite a lot, apparently. Gambling debts. Father was livid. He said Victor would 'learn the consequences.' I thought he'd calm down, but then the solicitor came last week...

clue.text: Margaret confirms a huge argument 3 weeks ago. Victor took estate money for gambling debts. Father threatened 'consequences' and then called the solicitor.

initial.prompt: Hartley stands stiffly in the hallway, hands clasped behind his back. He has served the Blackwood family for twenty-three years. His composure is impeccable, but his jaw is clenched tight.

choices.text: You found the body. Walk me through it.
choices.response: At approximately quarter past ten, I went to offer Lord Blackwood his nightcap — a habit of ours. The study door was locked from the inside. I knocked several times. No answer. I fetched Lady Eleanor and together we forced the door. His lordship was slumped over the desk. The brandy glass was on the desk, half finished. I noticed the bruise on the back of his head immediately.

clue.text: Study door was locked from inside when body was found. Hartley and Lady Eleanor forced it open.

choices.text: Who had access to the study today?
choices.response: Lord Blackwood kept his study locked and carried the only key on his person. However, I do keep a spare key in the butler's pantry — for emergencies. To my knowledge, no one else knows about it. Except... well, Mrs. Pemberton has seen me use it to clean the study.

clue.text: A spare study key exists in the butler's pantry. Only Hartley and Mrs. Pemberton know about it.

choices.text: When did you last see Lord Blackwood alive?
choices.response: I served dinner at seven. Afterward, Lord Blackwood retired to his study as usual — that was approximately half past eight. I brought him his brandy at that time. The decanter was full — I'd topped it up from the cellar stores that afternoon.

clue.text: Hartley last saw Lord B alive at 8:30 PM. Brought brandy and a freshly topped decanter.

choices.text: Is there anything about this evening that seemed unusual?
choices.response: Two things. First, Lord Blackwood asked me to post a letter tomorrow morning — marked 'urgent' and addressed to his solicitor. I still have it in the pantry. Second, Dr. Crawford arrived uninvited at about half past eight. Said he was passing by and the storm forced him to seek shelter. But Blackwood Manor is not on the way to anywhere.

clue.text: Lord B gave Hartley an urgent letter to his solicitor the night he died. Crawford arrived uninvited at 8:30.

ask_hartley_drawing_room.prompt: You ask Hartley about Lady Eleanor's whereabouts.

choices.text: Lady Eleanor says she was in the drawing room all evening. Can you confirm?
choices.response: I passed through the drawing room several times. Lady Eleanor was there at eight when I served after-dinner coffee. But when I passed through again at approximately nine o'clock, the room was empty. She returned sometime before half past nine — I saw her there when I went to stoke the fire. That's roughly thirty minutes unaccounted for.

clue.text: Lady Eleanor was NOT in the drawing room between 9:00–9:30 PM. She has a 30-minute gap in her alibi.

ask_hartley_decanter.prompt: You ask about the brandy decanter.

choices.text: You refilled the decanter that afternoon. Could anyone have tampered with it?
choices.response: The decanter was in Lord Blackwood's locked study. Only he and I — with the spare key — had access. Unless... well, the decanter was in the cellar before I brought it up. Anyone could have accessed the cellar during the day. It isn't locked. And now that I think of it, I saw Mrs. Pemberton coming up from the cellar at around four o'clock. She said she was fetching wine for the evening meal.

clue.text: The brandy was in the unlocked cellar before Hartley brought it up. Mrs. Pemberton was seen in the cellar at 4 PM.

ask_hartley_victor_clothes.prompt: You ask Hartley about Victor's clothing.

choices.text: Did you notice anything about Victor's appearance after dinner?
choices.response: Now that you mention it — Master Victor changed his shirt after dinner. I found his original shirt in the laundry hamper. There was a stain on the cuff. I assumed it was wine, but looking at it more carefully... it was darker. Reddish-brown. I haven't touched it — it's still in the hamper.

clue.text: Victor changed his shirt after dinner. The original had a dark reddish-brown stain on the cuff. Still in the laundry hamper.

initial.prompt: Dr. Crawford, 55, sits in the armchair adjusting his spectacles. His medical bag is at his feet, and his hands are remarkably steady for a man in a house with a fresh corpse.

choices.text: You examined the body. What can you tell me?
choices.response: Reginald died between nine and ten o'clock. Cause of death was poisoning — I could smell bitter almonds on his lips. Potassium cyanide, almost certainly, administered through the brandy. But here's the peculiar thing: there's also a significant contusion on the back of his skull. It was inflicted before death but wouldn't have been fatal on its own. Someone hit him, and then he was poisoned — or the poison was already working when he was struck.

clue.text: Death by cyanide poisoning in brandy (9-10 PM). Also a non-fatal blow to the back of the skull inflicted before death. Two attacks?

choices.text: What brings you to the manor tonight?
choices.response: I was returning from a house call in the village when the storm hit. Blackwood Manor was the nearest shelter. I arrived around half past eight and Hartley let me in. Reginald was already in his study. I sat in the parlour and read until the... unpleasantness.

clue.text: Dr. Crawford says he arrived at 8:30 PM seeking shelter from the storm. Claims he sat reading in the parlour.

choices.text: As the family doctor, did Lord Blackwood confide in you?
choices.response: I've been the family physician for fifteen years. Reginald told me things he told no one else. He was... worried. About his son's debts, about the estate's future. Last month he asked me a strange question — he asked about poisons. What common household substances could be lethal. I thought it academic curiosity. Now I wonder if he suspected someone was trying to poison him.

clue.text: Lord B asked Dr. Crawford about lethal poisons last month. He may have suspected someone was trying to poison him.

choices.text: You seem remarkably calm for a man whose patient was just murdered.
choices.response: I'm a physician, Detective. I've seen death more times than I care to count. But if you're suggesting I'm unmoved — I assure you, I am devastated. Reginald was not just a patient. He was a friend. And he was going to help me with... a personal matter. That help dies with him, I'm afraid.

clue.text: Lord B was going to help Crawford with a 'personal matter.' That help dies with Lord B.

ask_crawford_study_visit.prompt: You ask Dr. Crawford about being in the study.

choices.text: Someone heard voices in the study around 9 PM. Were you in there?
choices.response: ...Yes. I went to speak with Reginald privately at about nine o'clock. I wanted to discuss my personal situation — I owe money, Detective. Quite a lot. Medical malpractice settlement. Reginald had agreed to loan me the funds. I was in his study for perhaps ten minutes. He was alive and well when I left. The brandy glass was already on his desk, half poured. He hadn't drunk from it yet.

clue.text: Crawford admits he was in the study at 9 PM for about 10 minutes. Lord B was alive. The brandy was poured but not yet drunk.

ask_crawford_locked_room.prompt: You ask about the locked study door.

choices.text: The study was locked from inside. How do you explain that?
choices.response: The study has a spring lock — it can be set to lock automatically when the door closes. Reginald sometimes engaged it when he wanted privacy. If someone left the study and pulled the door firmly shut, it would lock behind them. The killer didn't need to have the key to lock it — only to enter.

clue.text: The study has a spring lock that auto-locks when the door shuts. The killer only needed the key to get IN, not to lock it afterward.

ask_crawford_uninvited.prompt: You press Crawford about his unannounced arrival.

choices.text: Hartley says you arrived uninvited. Blackwood Manor isn't on the way to anywhere. Why were you really here?
choices.response: You're right. I didn't come because of the storm. I came because I received a telephone call from Reginald at six o'clock — before the lines went down. He said he needed to see me urgently. He sounded frightened. He said, 'I think someone in this house is trying to kill me, Henry.' I drove straight here. But by the time I arrived and made it to the study at nine... I was too late to prevent anything.

clue.text: Lord B telephoned Crawford at 6 PM saying 'someone in this house is trying to kill me.' Crawford came immediately.

initial.prompt: Mrs. Pemberton, the housekeeper of thirty years, wrings her hands in the kitchen. She's a stout, grey-haired woman who knows every secret this house holds — or so the servants say.

choices.text: Where were you this evening, Mrs. Pemberton?
choices.response: I was in the kitchen all evening preparing tomorrow's meals and tidying up after dinner. I didn't leave the kitchen wing until I heard the commotion at quarter past ten. The kitchen is on the far side of the house from the study — I wouldn't have heard anything.

clue.text: Mrs. Pemberton was in the kitchen all evening. Kitchen is far from the study.

choices.text: You've served this family for thirty years. Any skeletons in the closet?
choices.response: Every great house has its secrets, Detective. But I'll tell you one thing — Lord Blackwood was not the saint everyone paints him as. He could be cruel when crossed. And there's the matter of the letters.

clue.text: Mrs. Pemberton says Lord B 'could be cruel when crossed.' References mysterious letters.

choices.text: You mentioned letters. What letters?
choices.response: For the past three months, Lord Blackwood has been receiving letters with no return address. Each time he read one, he'd go pale and lock himself in his study for hours. I saw one of them on his desk once — I didn't read it, but I noticed it was typed, not handwritten. And it smelled faintly of lavender perfume. Lady Eleanor wears lavender. But so does Miss Margaret.

clue.text: Lord B received anonymous typed letters for 3 months that disturbed him greatly. They smelled of lavender — worn by both Lady Eleanor and Margaret.

choices.text: Hartley mentioned a spare key to the study. Do you know about it?
choices.response: Hartley's spare key? Of course I know. I've used it myself to clean the study when his lordship was away. But I haven't touched it in weeks, I swear. Although... I noticed the key wasn't hanging in its usual spot last Thursday. It was back by Friday morning. Someone borrowed it.

clue.text: The spare study key went missing last Thursday and reappeared Friday. Someone borrowed it — time enough to make a copy.

ask_pemberton_key.prompt: You ask more about who might have taken the spare key.

choices.text: Who could have taken the spare key last Thursday?
choices.response: Anyone in the household, really. But I remember that Thursday clearly because Victor came down to the kitchen asking for headache powder. He was in the butler's pantry area — right where the key hangs. And Lady Eleanor asked me to fetch silver polish from the same pantry that afternoon. Either could have taken it.

clue.text: Both Victor AND Lady Eleanor were near the butler's pantry where the spare key hangs on Thursday — when it went missing.

ask_pemberton_cellar.prompt: You ask Mrs. Pemberton about the cellar.

choices.text: You were seen in the cellar at 4 PM. The brandy was stored there.
choices.response: I fetch wine from the cellar every day for dinner — it's part of my duties! But yes, I saw the brandy decanter there too. And I'll tell you something else: I saw a small glass vial on the cellar shelf that I'd never seen before. Brown glass, no label. It was gone the next time I went down. I thought Hartley had moved it, but I never asked.

clue.text: Mrs. Pemberton saw an unfamiliar brown glass vial on the cellar shelf near the brandy. It disappeared afterward.

ask_pemberton_crawford_debts.prompt: You ask about Dr. Crawford's situation.

choices.text: What do you know about Dr. Crawford's financial troubles?
choices.response: Everyone knows Dr. Crawford is in deep water. A patient's family sued him two years ago — negligence, they said. The settlement nearly bankrupted him. Lord Blackwood promised to bail him out, but I overheard them arguing about it last week. Lord Blackwood said he'd changed his mind — that he 'couldn't afford to help everyone who came begging.' Crawford was furious. I've never seen a man go so red in the face.

clue.text: Lord B REFUSED Crawford's loan request last week after initially promising it. Crawford was furious. He has a malpractice settlement to pay.

solution.reveal_narrative:
You gather everyone in the drawing room. The fire crackles as six pairs of eyes watch you pace before the mantelpiece.

'The killer,' you begin, 'is someone who stood to lose everything. Lord Blackwood discovered that his son, Victor, had been embezzling from the family estate to cover gambling debts. Three weeks ago they argued. Lord Blackwood threatened consequences — and last week, he summoned his solicitor to change his will.'

Victor rises from his chair. 'That doesn't prove—'

'Last Thursday, the spare key to the study went missing from the butler's pantry. You were there that afternoon, Mr. Blackwood, asking for headache powder. You took the key and had a copy made — returning the original by Friday.'

You continue: 'You knew your father drank from the study decanter every evening. The brandy was stored in the unlocked cellar before being brought up. A small brown glass vial appeared on the cellar shelf and vanished — cyanide, purchased under a false name, I suspect forensics will confirm.'

'At nine o'clock, after Dr. Crawford left the study, you used your copied key to enter. Your father confronted you — you struck him on the back of the head in a moment of panic. But the poison was already in the brandy. You fled, changed your stained shirt, and tried to establish an alibi in the library — but Margaret saw you leaving the study at 9:20.'

Victor's whisky glass slips from his fingers and shatters on the floor.

'Lord Blackwood knew someone in this house wanted him dead — he even telephoned Dr. Crawford in fear. But it wasn't revenge or hatred that drove you, Victor. It was self-preservation. If the new will went through, you would lose everything — the inheritance, the trust, your position in society. With your father dead before the solicitor received that urgent letter, the old will remains in effect. And you inherit it all.'

Victor collapses into his chair. Lady Eleanor turns her face away. The storm outside begins to break.

Case closed.
